- Material infrastructure: physical capital stock — pipelines, power lines, substations, storage, roads, ports, LNG terminals.
- Institutional infrastructure: legal framework, regulators, standards, market rules (Energiewirtschaftsgesetz, EU directives, Bundesnetzagentur, unbundling, DVGW, entry-exit model).
- Immaterial infrastructure: human capital — education, qualification, know-how, health, mobility, willingness to work.
- Jochimsen's classification. Point: infrastructure is not just steel in the ground — a pipeline needs a legal access regime and skilled people to run it.

- Weakness of rate-of-return (cost-based) regulation, opposite of incentive-based regulation.
- Firm earns a fixed % return on invested capital → profit rises with the capital base → over-invests, uses excess capital, distorts factor mix toward capital.
- = systematic gold-plating.
- Also under cost-based regulation: no incentive to cut operating costs or allocate factors efficiently; regulator can't easily tell necessary from unnecessary investment.
- Fix: incentive-based regulation (price cap, revenue cap, yardstick competition) decouples revenue from the firm's own costs.

- IDEAL: high security of supply, high sustainability, low price.
- REAL: price corner pulled outward (price is high); security of supply and sustainability only reach medium level — smaller, lopsided polygon.
- Reading: system currently pays a high price without full security of supply or sustainability.
- Gap between the two figures = political agenda (market design, network regulation, subsidy/tender instruments).
- Every corner pushed outward has to be paid for on another axis.

- Sketch: x-axis distance along pipeline, y-axis pressure; sawtooth line — steady drop from friction, jump up at each compressor station; mark minimum allowed pressure and maximum design pressure.
- Compressors maintain pressure: gas flows only along a pressure gradient, friction erodes it, so throughput collapses after a few hundred km without re-compression.
- Typical figures: pipelines up to 6,000 km, diameter up to 1,400 mm, pressure up to 100 bar, stations every 80-500 km, driven by gas or electricity, using up to ~0.5% of throughput per 100 km.
- Capacity can be bought with more steel (larger diameter) or more compression (more stations) — economic trade-off between the two.
- Also needed at storage sites, to inject gas against reservoir pressure.

- x-axis: hours/year gas flows (constant 1.4 mln m³/h) → rightward means higher utilisation; y-axis: cost per m³ transported.
- All curves fall left to right: fixed cost (steel, laying, right of way) spread over more volume as utilisation rises.
- Small diameters turn back up at high utilisation: higher gas velocity needed → friction loss grows with velocity² → compression energy (variable cost) grows faster than fixed cost per unit falls.
- Cheapest diameter by region: 34-inch below ~2,500-3,000 h/a, 38-inch in the middle range, 44-inch from ~4,000 h/a onward (still falling at 8,000 h/a).
- Rule: high, steady throughput justifies a large diameter; low or seasonal throughput does not.

- Four pipeline lines = two pairs: offshore vs onshore, and within onshore: low-pressure vs high-pressure.
- Offshore steepest (~1 USD/MMBtu at 500 mi → ~4.4 at 2,600 mi): seabed laying needs special vessels, thicker/coated pipe, no intermediate compressor stations.
- Onshore high-pressure flattest, stays below LNG out to 4,500 mi: higher pressure moves more gas per diameter, longer compressor spacing.
- Onshore low-pressure reaches ~3.3 USD/MMBtu at 4,500 mi, overtaken by LNG at ~3,000 mi.
- LNG line starts high (~1.8-2 USD/MMBtu even at short distance: liquefaction/regasification is a fixed cost) but rises gently (cheap sea leg).
- Caption states capacity 10·10^9 m³/yr: comparison only holds at this capacity — pipeline and LNG both have strong but different economies of scale, so break-even distances shift with volume.

- 2016: Qatar largest (~77 MTPA) ahead of Australia (~57 MTPA).
- 2022 projection: Australia overtakes Qatar (~88 MTPA vs flat ~77); other established exporters barely move.
- New entrants: US ~11→~67 MTPA (largest absolute growth), Russia ~11→~28 MTPA — growth concentrated in two countries.
- 2016 utilisation spans ~0% to >100%: Qatar, Australia, Norway, Russia, PNG, Malaysia at/above 100%; weak spots Angola (~15%), Cameroon (~0%), US (~48%, new trains ramping up).
- Liquefaction is capital-intensive (42% of chain cost, mostly fixed) → specific cost is inversely proportional to utilisation.
- Near 100% = capital earning as planned; near 0% = capital serviced with no output, usually feedgas shortage, unrest or commissioning delay. Slightly >100% is normal (nameplate is a design value).

- Compensation of demand fluctuations: seasonal (fill in summer, empty in winter) and daily/hourly peak shaving — demand is temperature-driven, production/pipeline capacity stays close to flat.
- Compensation of supply fluctuations: substitutes when a field, pipeline or LNG cargo fails — security-of-supply function (EU/German filling obligation since 2022).
- (Economic) optimisation: trading asset — buy cheap, sell expensive.
F: p_supply + p_storage < p_sales
- Re-optimised as prices move → option value.
- Technical match: seasonal stores (depleted fields, aquifers: large volume, low rates) serve functions 1 and 2; salt caverns (small volume, high rates, several cycles/year) serve peak shaving and trading.

- Time swap: intended trade is buy at t1 (p_supply), sell at t2 (p_sales) via physical storage. Swap replaces it with two trades at the same hub: sell at t1 (p1), buy back at t2 (p2).
F: p_supply − p1 < p_sales − p2
- Worthwhile vs. booking storage capacity if p2 − p1 < p_storage. Typically p1 < p2 (swap costs money) but can still beat the storage fee, with no physical asset needed.
- Intrinsic value: risk-free value locked in today from the forward curve — summer/winter spread minus storage cost, capped by injection/withdrawal rates; zero if spread < storage cost.
- Extrinsic value: extra optional value from re-optimising as prices move — monetises volatility, grows with volatility and cycling rate.
F: storage value = intrinsic value + extrinsic value
Note: the slides show the time swap but never use the terms "intrinsic"/"extrinsic value" — standard definitions used here.

- May 2020: ~3 €/MWh → summer 2022: >300 €/MWh — factor ~100 in two years.
- Covid 2020: demand collapse while supply kept flowing, storages filled early → price fell to near variable-cost floor.
- Autumn 2021: Russian pipeline flows throttled, Gazprom-controlled German storages left unfilled → Europe entered winter short, forward curve priced in scarcity.
- After Feb 2022: lost Russian volumes replaced by LNG bought against Asia; filling mandates forced buying regardless of price → inelastic demand meets inelastic supply.
- Not a cost-based price — a scarcity price rationing demand until industrial consumers stopped buying.

- Crude side (above refinery): Production → Refinery mainly by pipeline (central trunk); fed by ships (cargoes) harbour-to-harbour and rail station-to-station.
- Products side (below refinery): refinery → harbour-to-barges, station-to-rail, station-to-truck.
- Asymmetry: crude arrives in few, large, continuous streams → large-unit, low-cost modes (pipeline, tanker); products go to many small, dispersed customers → small-unit, flexible modes (barge, rail, truck) dominate.
- Refinery is the funnel between the two: few large flows in, many small flows out → transport cost per barrel rises downstream of it.
- Every mode change needs a node (harbour, station, tank farm) — where storage, quantity/quality measurement and ownership transfer happen.

- Two drivers: ambitious RES expansion targets + decentralisation of energy systems → structural rearrangement needed.
- Challenges: capacity overloads despite growing regional imbalance between production and consumption; power flow reversion and voltage stability problems in distribution grids; growing share of market players not driven mainly by economic criteria (behavioural aspects); overarching — maintain security of supply and system stability.
- Options: grid expansion, build-up of reserve capacity, more electricity export/import, storage and/or demand response, RES injection management (curtailment of excess generation).

Correct: salt caverns — conversion to hydrogen is feasible (impermeable, chemically inert, sterile rock salt), at the cost of ~80% less working gas volume than natural gas; depleted fields/aquifers are porous, hydrogen suitability not proven (168 TWh salt cavern vs 94 TWh porous storage in Europe).

- Jochimsen (1966): infrastructure = entirety of material, institutional and personnel facilities/conditions available to the division-of-labour economy

- Three types: material, institutional, immaterial

- Order: primary → secondary → end → usable energy
- Primary: naturally occurring, unconverted (coal, lignite, oil, gas, uranium, renewables)
- Secondary: from conversion in power plants/refineries, with conversion losses (electricity, district heat, heating oil, gasoline)
- End energy: reaches the consumer after distribution losses (the kWh on the meter)
- Usable energy: after the final conversion in the device (light, heat, mechanical work)
- Example: lignite (primary) → power-plant electricity, ~40% efficiency (secondary) → socket after grid losses (end) → light from the lamp (usable); each step loses efficiency

- Five traits: high capital requirements, external effects, economies of scale, step costs, high fixed-cost share.
- Economies of scale: average unit cost falls as output grows - fixed cost spread over more units, and pipe capacity grows faster than the steel needed. Basis of the natural monopoly.
- Step costs: capacity is added only in discrete jumps (pipe diameter, compressor size), so new capacity sits under-utilised until demand catches up.

Sub-additive
Cost function property: one firm can serve the whole market cheaper than several firms could - typically from high fixed cost / low marginal cost, often together with economies of scale.

- Economies of scale: average unit cost falls as output rises.
- Internal: advantage inside the firm - specialisation, technology, bargaining power. E.g. a 35,000 km TSO spreads control-centre and maintenance costs further and buys transformers in bulk.
- External: advantage outside the firm, industry- or region-wide - skilled labour, shared infrastructure. E.g. the Ruhr pipeline-engineering cluster, or a port region with existing LNG berths and know-how.
- Both raise profit and market share; in infrastructure they are the economic root of the natural monopoly.

- Pipeline cost rises ~linearly with distance: steel, right-of-way, a compressor station every 80-500 km.
- LNG chain: high fixed cost at both ends - liquefaction 42% of chain cost, storage/regasification 27% - but the sea leg (20%) is cheap and barely grows with distance.
- The cost curves cross: beyond a break-even distance LNG is cheaper. LNG (~2-2.5 US$/MMBtu) undercuts an offshore pipeline from ~1,000 miles and a low-pressure onshore line from ~3,000 miles; only a high-pressure onshore line stays competitive to ~4,500 miles.
- Strategic edge: LNG is not tied to one route - diversifies supply, reaches markets no pipeline does, avoids transit countries, allows cargo arbitrage. Pipelines still win at short distance and steady high volumes.
Note: LNG is liquefied natural gas (~-162 °C), not gaseous - liquefaction shrinks its volume by a factor of ~600, which is what makes sea transport possible.

- Chain: gas field -> processing -> pipeline -> liquefaction -> LNG tanks/loading terminal -> carrier -> receiving terminal/tanks -> regasification -> pipeline -> gas utilities/power station.
- As transport: gas in, gas out. Liquefaction (cooling to ~-162 °C, ~600-fold volume reduction) only enables sea transport; nothing is added, so it competes with pipelines on delivered cost.
- As a product: LNG has its own spec, price benchmarks and contracts (FOB, DES, charterparties) and serves uses pipeline gas can't (bunkering, small-scale LNG, power ships) - the same molecule ends up priced 7.8-12.8 USD/MMBtu depending on the end product.

- Sub-additive cost function (economies of scope/scale, sunk costs) → natural monopoly by definition.
